requirements.lead_text: Handling a First Aid Emergency. Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Handling a First Aid Emergency. Do the following: (a) Explain the steps necessary to assess and handle a first aid emergency, including a safety evaluation of the scene. (b) Tell how you would obtain emergency medical assistance from your home and from a remote location on a wilderness camping trip. (c) Demonstrate the precautions you must take to reduce the risk of transmitting an infection between you and the victim while administering first aid, including the safe disposal of used first aid supplies. (d) Demonstrate evaluation of and management of a patient's airway and breathing. (e) Demonstrate a thorough examination of an accident victim. (f) Discuss why shock is an emergency. (g) Define the term triage and describe examples of triage situations that you may encounter.

requirements.lead_text: Preparing for First Aid Emergencies. Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Preparing for First Aid Emergencies. Do the following: (a) Obtain a copy of the Scout Annual Health and Medical Record and discuss the importance of the form including information on immunizations, allergies, medications, health history, and medical examinations to providing first aid at Scouting events. (b) Using checklists provided in the First Aid merit badge pamphlet or ones approved by your counselor, do the following: (1) Assemble a personal first-aid kit for hiking and backpacking. Demonstrate the proper use of each item in your first-aid kit to your counselor. (2) With your counselor, inspect a unit, home, vehicle, or camp first-aid kit and discuss your findings.

requirements.req_text: Wounds with No External Bleeding. Describe the symptoms and signs of, show first aid for, and explain prevention of these wounds: (a) Closed wounds, such as a bruise (contusion) or a hematoma (b) Superficial, partial thickness, and full thickness thermal (heat) burns or scalds (c) Chemical burns (d) Electrical burns (e) Sunburn (f) Snow blindness (g) Immersion foot, frostnip, frostbite, and ice burns (h) Abrasions, such as chafing and rope burns (i) Blisters on the hands, feet, buttocks, and shoulders (j) Puncture wounds from splinters, rope splinters, nails, and fish hooks (k) Rash from poisonous plants (l) Bug bites of chiggers, ticks, mosquitoes, and biting gnats (m) Bee stings (n) Bites of spiders (o) Sting of a scorpion (p) Bite of a pet or wild mammal or human (q) Bite of a venomous snake

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Wounds with No External Bleeding): Inspect yourself daily, especially the hairy parts of your body, and immediately remove any ticks you find (p. 14).
Step 2 (Wounds with No External Bleeding): Ticks bury their heads beneath the skin of their victims (p. 14).
Step 3 (Wounds with No External Bleeding): To remove a tick, with gloved hands, grasp it with tweezers close to the skin and gently pulluntil it comes loose (p. 14).
Step 4 (Wounds with No External Bleeding): Don't squeeze, twist, or jerk thetick, as doing so could leave its mouthparts stillburied in the skin (p. 14).

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Breathing Emergencies): If an ear or cheek is frozen, remove a glove and warm the injury with the palm of your hand (p. 61).
Step 2 (Breathing Emergencies): Slip a frostnipped hand under your clothing and tuckit beneath an armpit (p. 61).
Step 3 (Breathing Emergencies): Treat frostnipped toes by putting the victim's bare feet against the warm skin of your belly (p. 61).
Step 4 (Breathing Emergencies): The human body is 70 percent water, which is essential tomaintain our body temperature (p. 61).

Heart Attack Principle 2: A person who is exposed to cold environmentalconditions and loses body heat faster than it can be generated will be in grave danger (p. 59).
Heart Attack Principle 3: The person's body temperature maybecome too low to support life (p. 59).
Heart Attack Principle 4: Likewise, a person whose bodyhas overheated and cannot cool itself sufficiently may die if fastemergency medical care cannot be found (p. 59).

Step 2 (Heart Attack): Hypothermia occurs when a person's body is losing more heatthan it can generate (p. 59).
Step 3 (Heart Attack): It is a danger for anyone who is notdressed warmly enough, although exposure to cold is seldom the only cause (p. 59).
Step 4 (Heart Attack): Dehydration is a common contributing factor to hypothermia (p. 59).

pamphlet_excerpts: Miscellaneous Conditions: Cold- and Heat-Related Conditions and Injuries Heatstroke Heatstroke, much more serious than heat exhaustion, canlead to death if not treated immediately (p. 63).
Miscellaneous Conditions Principle 2: Left untreated, heatexhaustion can develop into heatstroke (p. 63).
Miscellaneous Conditions Principle 3: In heatstroke, the body's cooling system begins to fail and the person's core temperature rises to life-threatening levels (above 105 degrees) (p. 63).
Miscellaneous Conditions Principle 4: One type of heatstroke develops in young, healthy people from dehydration and overexertion in hot weather, especially in highhumidity (p. 63).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Miscellaneous Conditions): The first sign of true heat stroke is often collapse (p. 63).
Step 2 (Miscellaneous Conditions): On a hot day, if someone collapses without warning, you mustconsider heatstroke (p. 63).
Step 3 (Miscellaneous Conditions): The other type of heatstroke usually happens in elderlypeople when the weather is very hot, especially with highhumidity (p. 63).
Step 4 (Miscellaneous Conditions): The signals are similar to exercise-related heatstrokeexcept that the skin is hot and dry because there is no sweating (p. 63).

requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) Visit an emergency medical station house or training center in person. From the medical first responders that you meet during your visit, learn about how they serve their community and about their careers. Discuss with your counselor what you learned during your tour and interviews. (b) Interview an emergency medical services professional about their work. Learn about how they chose this career and about their duties. Discuss what you learned with your counselor and whether you might be interested in this career. (c) Identify three career opportunities that would use skills and knowledge in emergency medical services. Pick one and research the training, education, certification requirements, experience, and expenses associated with entering the field. Research the prospects for employment, starting salary, advancement opportunities, and career goals associated with this career. Discuss what you learned with your counselor and whether you might be interested in this career. (d) Identify how you might use the skills and knowledge in the field of emergency medical services to pursue a personal hobby and/or healthy lifestyle. Research the additional training required, expenses, and affiliation with organizations that would help you maximize the enjoyment and benefit you might gain from it. Discuss what you learned with your counselor and share what short-term and long-term goals you might have if you pursued this.

pamphlet_excerpts: First Aid Careers and Pathways: Visit an emergency medical station house: Moving an Ill or Injured Person The decision to move an accident victim should be made carefully (p. 25).

First Aid Careers and Pathways Principle 2: Visit an emergency medical station house Principle 2: In many cases, there will be emergency medicalcrews, fire department personnel, or others with specialequipment and training who will transport (p. 25).

First Aid Careers and Pathways Principle 3: Visit an emergency medical station house Principle 3: If, however, someone is in danger from fire, smoke, water, electrical hazards, poisonous gases, exposure, or other immediate danger, you must move (p. 25).

First Aid Careers and Pathways Principle 4: Visit an emergency medical station house Principle 4: Youmight also need to move an injured person in order to give thatperson proper care, or reach another victim (p. 25).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (First Aid Careers and Pathways): Step 1 (Visit an emergency medical station house): Move the persononly as far as is necessary, and do not endanger yourself (p. 25).

Step 2 (First Aid Careers and Pathways): Step 2 (Visit an emergency medical station house): Sometimes you will find that a victim's injuries are minorenough that the person can move with some assistance (p. 25).

Step 3 (First Aid Careers and Pathways): Step 3 (Visit an emergency medical station house): Before attempting to move someone, make sure the person is notsuffering from any of the following conditions (p. 25).

Step 4 (First Aid Careers and Pathways): Step 4 (Visit an emergency medical station house): When time is critical, you might need to decidebetween moving the person to a place where they can get careor waiting for help to come (p. 25).

patrol_quiz_bank.question: While working on First Aid Requirement 8d(2)_q5 (Elastic Wrap and Cravat Bandages (Check 5)), your patrol encounters a decision point on proper procedure. According to the First Aid Merit Badge Pamphlet, which action is correct?
options: A. Straighten an angled fracture or dislocated joint in the field before applying a splint.
B. Defer all Elastic Wrap and Cravat Bandages (Check 5) measurements and safety checks until after the field session concludes.
C. Splint fractures and dislocations in the exact position found, immobilize the joints above and below the injury with a SAM or rigid.
D. Substitute uncalibrated equipment and unverified assumptions in place of the First Aid pamphlet procedure.
choices: A. Straighten an angled fracture or dislocated joint in the field before applying a splint.
B. Defer all Elastic Wrap and Cravat Bandages (Check 5) measurements and safety checks until after the field session concludes.
C. Splint fractures and dislocations in the exact position found, immobilize the joints above and below the injury with a SAM or rigid.
D. Substitute uncalibrated equipment and unverified assumptions in place of the First Aid pamphlet procedure.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. Splint fractures and dislocations in the exact position found, immobilize the joints above and below the injury with a SAM or rigid.
